Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II Bldg, EDSA corner Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY DILG OPINION NO. 28 S. 2010 09 March 2010 VICE-MAYOR MADILYN CABOTAJE-RAMIREZ Tayug, Pangasinan Dear Vice-Mayor Ramirez: This has reference to your earlier letter asking our legal opinion relative to your claim for back wages and other benefits appurtenant to your position after you won in the election protest. In reply to your query, we answer in the negative. Well-settled is the rule that a person acquires public office either by appointment or by election. An appointment is the act or designation by the executive officer, board or body to where that power has been delegated, of the individual who is to exercise the functions of a given office (Mechem, Section log). On the other hand, an election "means the choice or selection of candidates to public office by popular vote through the use of the ba//ot, and the elected officials are determined through the wi// of the electorate. An election is the embodiment of the popular wi//, the expression of the sovereign power of the people. The winner is the candidate who has obtained a majority or p/ura/ity of valid votes cast in the election" (Rulloda vs. COMELEC, G.R. No. 154198, January go, 2003). There are instances however where one's acquisition of right or title to such public office would be challenged or questioned thereby giving rise to multiple and repetitious suits. In order to protect the public by insuring the orderly functioning of the government despite allegations of defect in title to office of the public officers, there is the so-called de jure doctrine/de facto doctrine in public office. In de iure doctrine, a person has the lawful right to the office in all respects, but who has either been ousted from it, or who has never actually taken possession of it. On the other hand, the de facto doctrine refers to the principle which holds that a person who, by the proper authority, is admitted and sworn into office is deemed to be rightfully in such office until, by judicial declaration in a proper proceeding, he is ousted therefrom, or his admission thereto is declared void (63,4 Am. Jur. gd 1081 as cited in the Law on Public Officers and Election Law, de Leon and de Leon, Jr., ed., p. 106). A de facto officer is thus defined by the Supreme Court in the case of Torres vs. Ribo 81 Phil 44 as one who has

-2- the reputation of being the officer that he assumes to be, and yet is not a good officer in point of law. He must have acted as officer for such length of time, under color of title and under such circumstances of reputation or acquiescence by the public and public authorities, as to afford a presumption of election or appointment, and induce people, without inquiry, and relying on the supposition that he is the officer he assumes to be, to submit to or invoke his action. Based on the foregoing, we can aptly say that you are a dejure officer since you, after the election protest was decided in your favor, has the lawful right to the office in all respects, but who has either been ousted from it, or who has never actually taken possession of it in conformity with the abovementioned definition of a de jure officer. On the other hand, the person who had been proclaimed as winner and had initially assumed the Office of the Vice-Mayor of Tayug but was later ousted through the Writ of Execution issued by COMELEC can be properly considered as a de facto officer since he/she, by the proper authority, is sworn to and allowed to assume the vice-mayoralty post, and is deemed to be rightfully in such office until, by judicial declaration in a proper proceeding, he/she is ousted therefrom, or his/her admission thereto is declared void in conformity with the abovementioned definition of a de facto officer. Coming now to your query, may we invite your attention to the pronouncements made by the Supreme Court in the cases of Rodriguez vs. Tant 91 Phil 724 and Malaluan vs. COMELEC G.R. No. 120193 March 6 1996. In the case of Rodriguez vs. Tan, supra., Carlos Tan was proclaimed as one of those elected as Senators by the COMELEC in the 11 November 1947 elections and immediately entered into the performance of the duties of the position, after taking his oath of office thereto. Eulogio Rodriguez filed an election protest before the Senate Electoral Tribunal and said body rendered a judgment declaring Rodriguez to have been duly elected to office. Thus, Rodriguez sought for the collection of salaries and allowances appurtenant to the office of the Senator during the time that Tan held the same. The Supreme Court decided in the following manner and we quote: "xxx There is no question that the defendant (Tan) acted as a de facto officer during the time he held the office of Senator. He was one of the candidates of the Liberal Party in the elections of Notæmber II, 1947, and uns proctairned as one of those who had been elected by the Commission on Elections and thereqßer he took the oath of office and immediately entered into the performance of the duties of the position. Having been thus duly proclaimed as Senator and having assumed qffice as required by taw. it cannot be disputed that defendant is entitled to the nsation emoluments and allowances which our co Constitution provides for the position (Article VI, Section 14). This is as it should be. This is in keeping with the ordinary course of etænts. This is simple justice. The emolument must o to the rson who rendered the service unless the contrary is provided. There is no atærment in the complaint that he is Zinked with anv irregularity vitiating his election. This is the policy and the rule that has been followed consistently in this jurisdiction in connection with positions

-3- held by persons who had been elected thereto but were later ousted as a result of an election protest. The right of the rsons elected to co nsation duri their incumbenc has been recognized. We cannot recall anu precedent wherein the contrary rule has been upheld." (Emphasis Supplied) The foregoing ruling of the Supreme Court was reiterated in the later case of Malaluan vs. COMELEC, supra. The Supreme Court held therein and we quote: "The long-standing rule in this jurisdiction is that notwithstanding his subsequent ouster as a result of an election protest, an elective official who has been proclaimed by the COMELEC as winner in an electoral contest and who assumed omce and entered into the performance of the duties of that omce, is entitled to the compensation, emoluments and allowances legally provided for the position. In view of the foregoing, we are of the opinion that you may no longer recover the salaries appurtenant to the Office of the Vice-Mayor during the time that said position was held by the person who had been proclaimed as winner and had initially assumed said office but was later ousted as a result of the election protests. We hope that we have addressed your concern accordingly. Very truly yours, By Authority of the Secretary: AT". JESUS . Director III, Le I Servi e Copy furnished: Regional Director Manual V.
